title: Vincent Ferrer (5 April)
hook: a Dominican preacher who walked from town to town calling people to repentance
tomorrow: John Baptist de La Salle (7 April)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis of Paola, the hermit who named his brothers the least. Your line was the least ones. What least thing did you do, unseen? Day nine hundred eighty.

Dust on a road, and a crowd coming over the hill. At the front, an old friar in a black and white habit, walking, or on a donkey when his legs give out. Behind him, people who left their villages to follow him to the next one: some singing, some weeping, some who came to watch and stayed. When they reach the town, someone builds him a platform in the square, because the church won't hold them all. He preaches for hours. Then the crowd moves on, and he moves with it. His name was Vincent Ferrer, and the road was his pulpit.
screen: `A CROWD COMING OVER THE HILL.` → `THE CHURCH WON'T HOLD THEM ALL.` → `THE ROAD WAS HIS PULPIT.`

segments.voice: Vincent was a Dominican from Valencia, in Spain, a scholar and a teacher, and for a while a man of the papal court. His world was split. The Church had rival popes, each with his own cardinals and followers, and Vincent stood loyally by one of them. Then, the story goes, he fell gravely ill and in a vision was sent out to preach. He left the court and took to the road, and spent the rest of his life walking across Spain, France, Italy and beyond, calling people to repentance, to turn back to God before judgment comes. Tradition tells that people who didn't share his language understood him anyway. Saint Paul, quoting the prophet Isaiah, writes in the Douay-Rheims: "How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace." Feet, notice. Not voices. His later choice was costly: he came to withdraw his support from the pope he had served, so that the split could be healed. His preaching also had a hard side. It came at a time of heavy pressure on Jewish communities in Spain, and historians still weigh his part in it; that belongs in the story too. He died far from home, still on the road. Look back and this has been a week of feet and hands: Frances of Rome closing her prayer book to serve, Clement Hofbauer at his dough, Nicholas Owen behind his hidden walls, Turibius on his mule, Dismas asking to be remembered, Francis of Paola at a king's bedside. Today, a pair of walking feet.
screen: `A SCHOLAR IN A SPLIT CHURCH.` · `SENT OUT TO PREACH ON THE ROAD.` · `HE GAVE UP HIS POPE TO HEAL THE SPLIT.` · `A HARD SIDE TO THE STORY TOO.` · then, large: `HOW BEAUTIFUL ARE THE FEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: preach with your life, no words needed. Settle, and breathe. The crowds on the road saw how Vincent lived, not only what he said. Think of the places your own feet will carry you today. The kitchen, the bus, the office, the school pickup line. Pick one. Ask what the people there would learn about what you love, only from watching you, with the sound off. Choose one small thing to do there that says it plainly: patience, a kind word, a door held open. If you pray, you can ask for that. If you don't, simply keep the picture. The bell holds the time.
Vincent Ferrer. A Dominican who left the papal court to walk from town to town, preaching repentance, until he died on the road.
Your line: walking preacher. Today, let your feet do the talking in one place you go. Day nine hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Vincent Ferrer's optional memorial on 5 April; the Dominicans honor him as a preacher of their order, and he is especially remembered in Valencia and in Vannes, in Brittany, where he died.

notes: Week-end look back: Days 974–979 named with their carries (Frances of Rome, Clement Hofbauer, Nicholas Owen, Turibius, Dismas, Francis of Paola). Confirm the carries match those days' final scripts.
Claims rule: no dates, years, crowd sizes or sermon counts spoken. 'Old friar' in the hook: confirm; cut if a Keeper prefers.
Vision during illness (at Avignon, Christ with Dominic and Francis): given as 'the story goes'. Gift of tongues given as 'tradition tells'.
Schism: he supported the Avignon claimant (Benedict XIII, Pedro de Luna) and later withdrew support (1416), helping end the schism. Confirm summary.
Hard side: his preaching coincided with pressure on Jews in Spain (Tortosa disputation era, conversions, segregation laws). Phrased neutrally; a Keeper and a historian should review this sentence.
